chunks: "I'd start from why I'm measuring. For protection I want current, temperature and supply voltage.
For control I want speed or position, and torque, which for a DC motor I can get from current because torque is roughly K t times current.
For health and efficiency I want input power, and over time trends like winding resistance, vibration and the current needed for the same job.
Current is the most useful single measurement. It tells me load, detects stall and shorts, and with the torque constant gives torque.
Temperature of the winding is the other critical one, because it's what actually kills motors.
Voltage matters on the supply side, both undervoltage and the overvoltage you get from regeneration, and at the motor terminals for back-EMF.
Speed and position come from an encoder, Hall sensors, a tachometer, or from back-EMF without a sensor.
For solenoids I'd add the stroke time and plunger position or at least detect when it's seated, because the current waveform shows a kink when the plunger moves.
If I want to get fancy: vibration or sound for bearing wear, and trend winding resistance, since copper's resistance rises with temperature, which gives winding temperature for free."
